Subject: Post-call: Performance / SLO follow-up — p95/p99 targets (hosted vs current provider)

Tom — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned on the p95/p99 qualification we discussed: 

Summary of Finlytics requirements (please correct if I got anything wrong):
- End-to-end p95 latency target: <= 300 ms for typical inference requests (prompt + 128 tokens output).
- End-to-end p99 target: <= 700 ms.
- Peak concurrency: sustained 50 concurrent requests with bursts up to 200 RPS (short windows).
- Average payload size: ~256 input tokens, expected output ~128 tokens.
- Streaming: client requires streaming-first-token within <= 150 ms for interactive flows; full-stream TTF should still meet p95 goals where possible.
- Throughput: baseline 20 rps sustained, 200 rps burst for batched workflows.

What we committed to provide from Redwood:
1) A short PoC load test (24-48h) comparing Hosted API against your current provider using a representative query set and traffic shape.
2) Measurement artifacts: p95/p99 histograms, per-request trace IDs, and sample traces for slow tails.
3) Config recommendations (batching, concurrency limits, streaming vs chunk size) and a proposed SLA band to align expectations.

Immediate next steps:
- Tom: please share your current provider p95/p99 histograms (CSV or traces) and a sample of representative requests (anonymized). Attachments are fine — we requested a small sample during the call.
- Finlytics engineering: confirm the 128-token output assumption and whether any requests require >512 tokens.
- Redwood (Marissa/Aditya): can you draft an initial PoC plan + test harness (tools, traffic shape, success criteria) by EOD tomorrow?

Attachment: we can accept your exported metrics as CSV/zip. I added our HubSpot deal link and a drive folder for artifacts in the metadata.

Thanks — want to make sure the PoC targets the right tail metrics and traffic shapes.

Best,

Laura — thanks for the recap and the clear next steps. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The numbers look right for our real-time UI flows: p95 <= 300ms, p99 <= 700ms is what the product team wants for sub-second interactions. For long-form batch scoring jobs we tolerate higher tail (p99 up to ~1.5s) but those will be routed differently.
- Burst behavior: we do have ~5-10 minute windows during end-of-day processing where traffic spikes to ~200 RPS; latency for those is less critical if we can route to a separate batch capacity.
- Token sizing: most interactive requests are ~150 input tokens / ~120 output tokens. We have a handful (~5%) of requests that exceed 512 tokens.

I've attached a small CSV export of our current provider's p95/p99 buckets for the last 7 days (finlytics_current_provider_metrics_20260224.csv) and a zip with a few sampled traces. The CSV has timestamp, request_type, latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, and concurrency at sample time. Let me know if the format works or if you need raw traces (we can redact PII).

Questions:
- Will Redwood's hosted offering support a mixed routing policy (interactive -> low-latency pool; batch -> higher-throughput lower-cost pool)? That was discussed briefly but we want to ensure the PoC reflects our routing mix.
- For streaming, how do you measure the p95/p99? Is it first-byte TTF for streaming or end-to-end that you report?

I'll loop in our infra lead if you need more detailed traces.

Thanks,
Tom

Tom / Laura — thanks for the artifacts, Tom. I pulled a quick pass over the CSV and the sample traces — helpful. A few technical notes and an initial PoC/test plan outline below.

Key technical considerations for p95/p99 across hosted vs current provider:
- End-to-end latency includes: client network RTT, API gateway/frontend, model decode time (compute), batching delays, and any queued work for concurrency throttling. We'll instrument traces with per-hop timestamps so we can attribute tail sources.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: for streaming-first-byte p95 we measure TTF for first token (this is what interactive UIs care about). For end-to-end p95/p99 we report full-response latency including decode. Streaming can reduce perceived latency (first token) but may not change total compute time for long outputs.
- Batching: larger batch sizes increase throughput but add batching delay; we'll tune batch windows and target batch sizes that meet p95 goals under your concurrency shape.
- Concurrency and autoscale: sustained concurrency 50 and bursts to 200 RPS are within our Dedicated pool assumptions; for hosted we can emulate similar routing using low-latency autoscale pools + overflow to burst capacity. We'll validate with load tests.

Proposed PoC/test harness (draft):
1) Representative query set: 200 unique prompts that reflect interactive and batch workloads (Tom to confirm).
2) Traffic profile: baseline 20 RPS sustained, 50 concurrent sustained, 200 RPS 5-minute bursts (50% interactive, 50% batch).
3) Metrics to collect: p50/p95/p99 histograms, first-byte TTF for streaming, per-request flame/trace, CPU/GPU utilization, batch sizes distribution, and error rates.
4) Test tools: wrk2 + custom client for streaming, distributed runners to emulate geographic RTTs.
5) Success criteria: hosted p95 <= 300ms and p99 <= 700ms for interactive traffic; streaming-first-token p95 <= 150ms. For any failure modes we produce root-cause traces and tuning plan.
6) Duration: 24-48 hours with three steady-state windows and two burst windows.

Next steps we need from Finlytics:
- Confirm the 200-prompt sample set and which prompts require >512 tokens.
- Confirm if you can share a short list of representative client RTTs (avg/95th) so we include network in the PoC.
- Approve the test window and we will provision a hosted test endpoint + test harness.

I can draft the PoC runbook and test configs today, then Marissa will coordinate scheduling.

Best,
Aditya Rao
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
